questions.stem: The United Nations defines a megacity as an urban area with a population of:
options: 50 million or more
10 million or more
1 million or more
5 million or more
questions.explanation: Megacities have at least 10 million people. Many other large cities are approaching this size, especially in Asia and Africa.

questions.stem: UN figures show the number of megacities rising from a handful in the 1970s to more than 30 today. Where are most of today's megacities?
options: Asia
Europe
Oceania
North America
questions.explanation: Asia holds most megacities, including Jakarta, Dhaka, Tokyo, Delhi and Shanghai. Africa and Latin America have several, while Europe and North America have few.

questions.stem: Most new megacities in recent decades have emerged in less developed countries. Which combination of processes best explains this?
options: low natural increase plus emigration to other countries
deindustrialisation plus the closure of urban factories
high natural increase plus large-scale rural-urban migration
falling birth rates plus migration from cities to rural areas
questions.explanation: Young populations with high birth rates, together with migrants seeking work and services, drive rapid urban growth in developing countries. Most developed countries urbanised earlier.

questions.stem: Which is a 'pull' factor drawing rural migrants to a megacity?
options: better access to jobs, schools and clinics
drought and crop failure in rural areas
lack of land for young farmers to inherit
conflict and insecurity in rural regions
questions.explanation: Pull factors attract people to a place. Drought, landlessness and conflict are push factors that drive people away from rural areas.

questions.stem: The Greater Jakarta urban region has spread well beyond the city's administrative boundary into neighbouring cities and districts. Why do estimates of megacity populations differ so much between sources?
options: only cities in developed countries are measured with consistent methods
sources draw the urban boundary differently, from city to region
megacities are never counted in national censuses, so all figures are estimates
populations of megacities change by half from one year to the next
questions.explanation: A megacity's population depends on whether the boundary is the administrative city, the continuous built-up area or the wider metropolitan region. UN figures revised in 2025 using a new method changed several rankings.

questions.stem: Rapid urban growth can be an opportunity for a country's development because megacities:
options: always have lower living costs than rural areas
need no new infrastructure as they grow
reduce the demand for energy and water
concentrate jobs, markets, skills and capital
questions.explanation: Agglomeration brings businesses, workers and customers together, raising productivity and incomes. Megacities often produce a large share of national output.

questions.stem: Which is a key risk of a megacity growing faster than its government can provide infrastructure?
options: a decline in traffic as people stop travelling within the city
informal settlements without water, sanitation or tenure
a surplus of housing, leaving many formal dwellings empty for years
falling population density as residents move to rural areas
questions.explanation: When growth outpaces formal housing and services, many people live in informal settlements with poor sanitation, insecure land rights and high exposure to hazards.

questions.stem: The informal economy in a megacity includes:
options: jobs in banks, government offices and large corporations
work in large factories with union contracts
professional services such as law and accounting
unregistered work such as street vending
questions.explanation: Informal work is unregulated and untaxed and often provides the main income for recent migrants. It is flexible but offers little security, protection or social support.

questions.stem: Many residents of informal settlements lack secure land tenure. Why does this matter for liveability?
options: residents are guaranteed government housing whenever they want it
secure tenure is only relevant to farmers in rural areas
lack of tenure means residents pay much higher property taxes
residents risk eviction and have little reason to invest
questions.explanation: Without legal rights to land, people can be evicted and are reluctant to improve housing. Governments are also less likely to provide services to settlements they do not recognise.

questions.stem: As a megacity spreads outwards, it converts farmland and wetlands on its fringe into housing and industry. This risk is described as:
options: rising population density in the centre
reforestation of the peri-urban fringe
changing land use and consumption of land
counterurbanisation from the inner city core
questions.explanation: Urban expansion consumes land, often fertile farmland and wetlands that store floodwater. This can increase flood risk and reduce local food production.

questions.stem: Many megacities are on coasts and river deltas. Why does this increase their risk from natural hazards?
options: coastal cities are always built far from any rivers or tidal water
dense populations are exposed to floods, surges and rising seas
coastal locations protect cities from cyclones, floods and storm surges
deltas are high and rocky, so cities there have no flood risk at all
questions.explanation: Ports and fertile deltas attracted settlement, but low-lying land is flood-prone. With millions of people and assets concentrated there, the potential for disaster is high.

questions.stem: Population densities in some informal settlements are very high. Which health risk is most closely linked to this?
options: reduced exposure to heat because buildings shade each other
rapid spread of infectious disease where sanitation is poor
lower rates of respiratory illness due to clean air
fewer cases of waterborne disease than in rural areas
questions.explanation: Crowding with poor sanitation and limited clean water allows diseases such as diarrhoea and tuberculosis to spread. Dense, hard-surfaced areas also tend to be hotter.

questions.stem: Compared with megacities in more developed countries, megacities in less developed countries more often face which challenge?
options: very slow population growth and empty housing stock
many residents without piped water or sewerage
an ageing population with a shrinking workforce
high rates of car ownership with low public transport use
questions.explanation: Rapid growth and limited funds leave many residents without basic services in less developed countries. Ageing and shrinking populations are more typical of megacities such as Tokyo or Osaka.

questions.stem: Tokyo, a megacity in a more developed country, has extensive flood defences and earthquake building codes but an ageing population. This shows that:
options: megacities in richer countries face no challenges of any kind
ageing populations only occur in less developed countries
earthquake risk only affects megacities in Africa
richer megacities face different challenges, not none
questions.explanation: Wealthier megacities can afford infrastructure and regulation, but face issues such as ageing, high housing costs and long commutes. All megacities face sustainability challenges.

questions.stem: Waste management is a major challenge in many megacities in less developed countries. Which is a common consequence?
options: too little waste, so recycling plants have no supply
waste is all exported, so no landfill is needed
waste collection reaches every household daily
rubbish blocking drains and canals, worsening floods
questions.explanation: Where collection is incomplete, waste is dumped in waterways, blocking drainage and raising flood and health risks. Informal waste pickers recover much recyclable material.

questions.stem: Which challenge is shared by megacities in both less and more developed countries?
options: traffic congestion and air pollution
the lack of any formal economy
no access to electricity anywhere
a population decline of over 50%
questions.explanation: Congestion and air pollution affect megacities everywhere, though their causes and responses differ. Lack of a formal economy or electricity is not true of megacities.

questions.stem: Climate change is expected to worsen challenges for megacities. Which combination is most likely for a low-lying tropical megacity?
options: no change in rainfall, sea level or temperature
heavier rainfall, rising seas and more extreme heat
less rainfall, falling seas and cooler temperatures
more snowfall, falling seas and longer winters
questions.explanation: Warming brings heavier downpours, sea level rise and more heatwaves, which the urban heat island makes worse. Poorer residents in exposed areas are most vulnerable.

questions.stem: A resilient city is one that can:
options: prevent every hazard from ever occurring
stop all population growth within its borders
rely entirely on aid after each disaster
absorb shocks, recover and adapt
questions.explanation: Urban resilience is the ability to withstand events such as floods or heatwaves, recover quickly and adapt to changing conditions, such as climate change.

questions.stem: China's 'sponge city' approach uses parks, wetlands, permeable paving and green roofs. Its main purpose is to:
options: replace all green space with concrete drainage channels
increase surface runoff to keep rivers flowing in winter
absorb, store and reuse rain to reduce flooding
pump all rainwater out to sea as quickly as possible
questions.explanation: Sponge city design lets rain soak in and be stored rather than running off hard surfaces, reducing flood peaks and helping water supply. It works with natural processes.

questions.stem: Bus rapid transit, with dedicated lanes and quick boarding, is used in megacities such as Jakarta and Bogotá. How does it support sustainability?
options: it is only suitable for small towns with few passengers
it moves many people cheaply, cutting congestion
it encourages more private car use by freeing up road space
it requires no road space, so it has no effect on traffic
questions.explanation: BRT provides high-capacity transport at lower cost than rail and can be built quickly. It reduces travel times and car use, though it still depends on good planning and integration.

questions.stem: Which response to informal settlements is generally regarded as more sustainable?
options: demolishing settlements and relocating residents far from jobs
ignoring settlements so that residents eventually leave the city
fencing settlements to stop them receiving any city services
upgrading settlements in place with services and secure tenure
questions.explanation: In-situ upgrading improves water, drainage, paths and tenure while keeping people near work and social networks. Forced relocation often breaks livelihoods and many people return.

questions.stem: Jakarta, Indonesia's largest city, lies on the north-west coast of which island?
options: Java
Sumatra
Borneo
Bali
questions.explanation: Jakarta is on the northern coast of Java, Indonesia's most populous island, on low-lying land crossed by many rivers flowing into the Java Sea.

questions.stem: UN figures published in 2025 ranked Greater Jakarta as the world's most populous urban area. Which processes have driven its growth?
options: emigration from Jakarta to other countries over recent decades
a fall in the birth rate to zero with no migration to the city
the movement of all Indonesians from cities to rural villages
natural increase and migration from across Indonesia
questions.explanation: Jakarta has grown through natural increase and migrants drawn by jobs and services, and the urban region has spread into neighbouring cities such as Bogor, Depok, Tangerang and Bekasi.

questions.stem: Parts of Jakarta, especially in the north, are sinking by several centimetres a year. What is the main cause of this land subsidence?
options: tectonic uplift of the island of Java
rising sea level pushing the land downwards
heavy rainfall compressing the soil
pumping of groundwater from beneath the city
questions.explanation: Many households and businesses pump groundwater because piped water does not reach them. Removing water from soft sediments makes the ground compact and sink, while the weight of buildings adds to it.

questions.stem: Why does land subsidence make Jakarta's flood risk much worse?
options: land sinks as seas rise, so more of the city lies below sea level
sinking land raises the city above the reach of high tides and storm surges
subsidence widens rivers, so they carry floodwater away more quickly
subsidence only affects buildings, not the city's exposure to flooding
questions.explanation: As parts of the city sink below sea level, seawater floods in at high tide and rivers cannot drain to the sea, so pumps and sea walls are needed. Sea level rise adds to the problem.

questions.stem: Many of Jakarta's rivers and canals are narrowed by settlements along their banks and blocked by rubbish. What effect does this have?
options: cleaner water, because settlements filter the river flow
reduced channel capacity, so heavy rain causes more flooding
increased channel capacity, so floods drain away faster
no effect, because rivers always carry the same amount of water
questions.explanation: Narrower, blocked channels hold less water, so floods overflow sooner. Riverbank settlements are also among the most exposed to flooding.

questions.stem: Which group in Jakarta is most vulnerable to flooding?
options: residents of high-rise apartments on the city's southern hills
office workers in air-conditioned towers in the business district
residents of gated estates with private pumps and sea walls
low-income residents of riverbank and coastal kampungs
questions.explanation: Poorer households often live in the most flood-prone places, have weaker housing and fewer resources to recover. Wealthier residents can afford safer locations and protection.

questions.stem: The Kampung Improvement Program, begun in Jakarta in 1969, is significant because it:
options: banned migrants from settling in Jakarta for the next fifty years
upgraded informal neighbourhoods with paths, drains and water in place
demolished all informal neighbourhoods and moved residents to the countryside
built a new capital city on the island of Borneo to replace Jakarta
questions.explanation: It was one of the earliest large slum upgrading programs, improving infrastructure in existing kampungs rather than clearing them, and became a model for other cities.

questions.stem: Indonesia passed a law in 2022 to move its national capital from Jakarta to Nusantara, in East Kalimantan on Borneo. Which reason is commonly given?
options: because Borneo has a larger population than Java
to ease pressure on crowded, sinking Jakarta and spread development
to move the government closer to Australia for trade purposes
because Jakarta has no flooding, congestion or environmental problems
questions.explanation: The move aims to relieve congestion and environmental pressure on Jakarta and to spread development beyond Java. Critics note Jakarta's millions of residents will still need solutions to flooding and subsidence.

questions.stem: Jakarta is building sea walls along its coast and upgrading pumps. Why do experts argue these alone will not solve its flooding?
options: sea walls make subsidence stop immediately along the coast
Jakarta's flooding comes only from the sea, never from rivers
pumps and sea walls are not used anywhere else in the world
subsidence continues unless groundwater pumping is cut
questions.explanation: If groundwater extraction continues, the land keeps sinking, and walls must keep being raised. Expanding piped water to reduce pumping tackles the cause.

questions.stem: Which proposed action would best address Jakarta's flooding challenge and improve liveability?
options: pave remaining green spaces so water flows faster into the sea
expand piped water to cut groundwater use, and clear rivers
pump more groundwater so that the city has more water to drain away
build more housing on riverbanks to raise the land with buildings
questions.explanation: Supplying piped water reduces the extraction driving subsidence, and clearing and widening channels, with fair resettlement or upgrading for affected residents, improves drainage.

questions.stem: Jakarta opened its first MRT (metro) line in 2019, adding to its TransJakarta bus rapid transit network. Which challenge do these mainly address?
options: traffic congestion and air pollution from vehicles
land subsidence caused by pumping groundwater
shortages of clean drinking water in kampungs
coastal flooding from storm surges and high tides
questions.explanation: Mass transit gives commuters an alternative to cars and motorcycles, easing congestion and pollution. Subsidence and water supply need different responses.

questions.stem: A student maps Jakarta's built-up area from satellite images taken in 1990 and 2020. This helps describe:
options: the number of people using the MRT each day
the cultural traditions of each neighbourhood
the nature and extent of urban growth
the income of each household in the city
questions.explanation: Comparing satellite images shows how far and in which directions the city has expanded, including onto farmland and wetlands. Incomes and travel need survey data.

questions.stem: Which data would best show whether Jakarta's responses are reducing flood impacts over time?
options: the length of new roads built on the city's outer fringe
area flooded and households affected in similar rainfall events
the number of new skyscrapers built in the central business district
the population of Jakarta at the most recent national census
questions.explanation: Effectiveness is judged by outcomes, comparing flood extent and impacts in events of similar rainfall, so that differences reflect management rather than weather.

questions.stem: Why is Jakarta a useful case study of the challenges facing megacities in less developed countries?
options: its population is shrinking quickly, as in many rich countries
it is located far from the coast, away from any natural hazards
it combines rapid growth, informal housing, hazards and service gaps
it has no informal settlements, so it shows a fully planned city
questions.explanation: Jakarta shows how rapid urbanisation, gaps in water and sanitation, informal housing and environmental hazards interact, and how planning responses try to improve liveability.
